paras: The threatened lynching of Ben Cunningham took place in upper Union County, South Carolina, in late May 1888, when a party pursued Cunningham, a Black tenant farmer accused of killing his landlord's sixteen-year-old son, Gunning Byers, amid 'much talk of lynching him.' Officers arrested Cunningham the next day and took him toward the courthouse, and a local correspondent later reported that Byers had survived. The case drew notice mainly through a Columbia dispatch that predicted Cunningham would never come to trial, an account the same correspondent called 'quite erroneous.'

Cunningham was a tenant on the farm of William Byers near Wilkinsville, whom the Greenville News described as one of the largest planters in that part of the county. According to the early reports, the two men had a dispute a few days before the attack, after which Cunningham swore vengeance against the whole Byers family.

On Thursday evening or Friday, about May 24 or 25, Gunning Byers, about sixteen, was struck in the head and badly wounded on his father's plantation. The Columbia dispatch and the Greenville News said Cunningham met him in the woods and struck him with an ax, and the dispatch called it a 'brutal murder.' Cunningham fled, and the dispatch, dated May 27, reported that a party was in pursuit and that he would 'doubtless never come to trial' unless the authorities reached him first.

A Spartanburg dispatch printed in the News and Courier on Monday gave a different picture. It said that Byers was resting quietly and rational on Saturday, and that the accused had been arrested at noon that day while hiding several miles from home. Officers then started toward the courthouse with him, and no paper reports that the pursuing party caught him or that any attempt was made to seize him.

Writing from Union County on June 4, the Yorkville Enquirer's correspondent 'Sigma' reported that Byers had been treated at once by Dr. M. J. Walker, who removed twenty-four fragments of skull, and that the patient was conscious and 'doing well.' The correspondent withheld further details because the matter would 'undergo a legal investigation,' but no report of a hearing, indictment or trial appears in the coverage.

The Atlanta Constitution printed the Columbia special on May 29 under the headlines 'Swift Vengeance Taken' and 'A South Carolina Desperado's Terrible Crime,' although the story reported no vengeance, only pursuit and talk of lynching. The same text ran unchanged in the Anderson Intelligencer on May 31 and, under the Constitution's headline, in the Charlotte Messenger on June 2. As late as June 4 the Savannah Morning News still reported that Cunningham had killed the youth, whom it called 'young William Byers.'

The Yorkville Enquirer, which drew on South Carolina sources and its own Union County correspondent, took a different line. On May 30 it set the Greenville News report of a fatal wound beside the dispatch announcing Cunningham's arrest, and a week later its Union County correspondent singled out the Constitution's account as 'quite erroneous,' comparing such reporters to Ananias and Sapphira.

Accounts differed on the weapon, the outcome and the accused's name. The early reports said Byers was struck with an ax and killed or fatally wounded, while the Union County correspondent, who said he had been shown the stone, wrote that Cunningham threw a stone of about four pounds from some twenty-eight yards and that Byers survived. The correspondent also named the accused 'Jerry Cunningham,' where every other report called him Ben.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Ben Cunningham
bases: The only mob element is a pursuing party and 'much talk of lynching' a Black man accused of killing a white youth (A1); officers arrested him the next day and no mob action against him is reported (A2), so this is a threatened lynching at most.

Cunningham was threatened with lynching by a pursuing party over an accused killing (A1), but he was reported arrested by officers and taken toward the Court House (A2), and no paper reports anyone killed by a mob; the supposed murder victim was later reported alive (A6).

The attack on young Byers is reported independently by the Columbia dispatch (A1), the Greenville News and a Spartanburg dispatch (A2), but the talk of lynching appears only in the Columbia dispatch, and a Union county correspondent called the published accounts, especially the Constitution's, 'quite erroneous' on the weapon and the outcome (A6).

accounts.label: Columbia special dispatch
accounts.gist: Cunningham, after swearing vengeance on the Byers family, killed young Byers with an ax in the woods and fled; a party was in pursuit and there was much talk of lynching him.

accounts.label: Greenville News and Spartanburg dispatch (via Yorkville Enquirer)
accounts.gist: Cunningham struck Byers with an axe, inflicting a wound expected to be fatal; a later dispatch said Byers was resting and rational and that the accused had been arrested and was being taken by officers to the Court House.

accounts.label: Union county correspondent
accounts.gist: Byers was struck above the left eye by a stone of about four pounds thrown from twenty-eight yards, walked home, was treated by Dr. Walker and was doing well; the matter would undergo legal investigation.

framing.detail: The Columbia special called it the 'brutal murder' of a 'white youth' by 'a negro', headlined it 'Swift Vengeance Taken', and predicted Cunningham would 'never come to trial' if the pursuers caught him, without endorsing or condemning that outcome.
The Anderson Intelligencer and the Charlotte Messenger reprinted the Columbia dispatch unchanged.
The Yorkville Enquirer's correspondent rebuked the press, comparing reporters to Ananias and Sapphira, and withheld details pending a legal investigation.
